1.1: 1.1 Argument. He reminds and instructs Titus about the establishment of the presbyterate and about spiritual conduct, and about avoiding heretics, who believe in Jewish traditions, writing to him from Nicopolis. Paul, a servant, etc. By condition, not however of sin in wretched servitude, but of God. Some by nobility, as Moses and David are called servants, and Mary handmaid. According to the faith of the elect. That is, which the elect of God hold or by which they are saved, and therefore through it one must labor the more.
1.2: 1.2 In hope of eternal life. This is the thing, this the fruit of the apostolic office. By this he commends that the apostolic office is not to be performed more lukewarmly. Before the ages, etc. Not a recent promise, but before the times of all the ages.
1.3: 1.3 He manifested. This was done at fitting times, namely the Word, that is the Son: This is eternal life.
1.4: 1.4 To my son according to the common faith. That is, the Catholic, not the private faith of anyone. Catholicon in Greek is called common or universal in Latin. For this cause. First he says what he ought to do and what sort of presbyters to appoint, beginning thus, for this cause. While he recalls this, he warns him to carry out as he had arranged for him.
1.5: 1.5 Presbyters. He says presbyters in the plural, not in the singular, so that the burden of pastoral care may be more easily borne, divided among many.
1.6: 1.6 Without reproach. If he had said, without sin, no one in the Church could rightly be ordained a minister. For many baptized believers are without reproach, but without sin in this life I would say no one; not because any sin remains that is not forgiven in baptism, but because in us who remain in the weakness of this life things do not cease to happen daily which are daily forgiven to those who pray faithfully. However strictly you examine even a very just man in this life, he is not without sin. The husband of one wife. (JEROME, Letter to Oceanus.) After baptism, etc., up to because it is to apostatize from the one God and go to the superstition of another. Having faithful children. That is, not even accused of luxury, or not subject to him. Otherwise there is no hope in him of correcting others, nor does he have the face to live with others of such kind.
1.7: 1.7 For it behooves. Such a man ought to be appointed: for it is necessary for the handling of the office that he be without reproach, that is, an irreproachable bishop. Here he openly shows that bishops were designated above by the name of presbyters.
1.9: 1.9 To reprove those who contradict. Those who contradict are not to be understood in one way; for very few contradict us by speaking, but many by living badly. Who dares to contradict the truth by speaking quite openly? Many contradict not with the tongue but with life: to reprove them is a good work, a great burden, a steep climb.
1.12: 1.12 One of them said. AUGUSTINE, book 2, Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets. This was Epimenides the Cretan, in whose books this is found, etc., up to is to be taken up for the ministry of the house of God.
1.14: 1.14 Commandments. Because the commandments of the law, after the truth was made manifest, are now commandments of men, not of God.
1.15: 1.15 To the pure all things are pure. They deny this because in the law Moses prohibited certain things and distinguished clean from unclean. But he did not wish this to be understood according to the natures which God created, but according to significations: all things, therefore, are clean to the clean according to nature; hence in Genesis: God saw all that he had made, and they were very good. According to significations certain things are unclean to the Jews: nor are all things suitable for us, either for the health of bodies or for the custom of human society.
1.16: 1.16 But by their deeds. If denial is made not only by the tongue but also by deeds, we certainly find many Antichrists, who confess Christ with the mouth and in their conduct dissent from him. Whoever denies Christ by deeds is an Antichrist. Such are all bad Catholics, who deny not by words but by deeds. Do not, then, be as though secure about the faith; join a right life to the right faith, that you may confess Christ both by teaching true things in words and by living well in deeds. For if you confess in words and not in deeds, the faith of such as these is properly the faith of demons.
2.1: 2.1 But speak the things which befit sound doctrine. These are the things that pertain to good morals.
2.2: 2.2 That the aged men be sober. CHRYSOSTOM. Old age has certain faults of its own and diseases which youth lacks. And old age itself is a disease, but there is in it besides a certain sluggishness and slowness, deep forgetfulness, dullness of the senses, and irascibility. For there are very many things which at such an age are hardly allowed to be done.
2.3: 2.3 In holy attire. That is, that their gait, movement, face, and speech may display holiness. Not given to much wine. For there are some women who, when the luxury of the body grows cold, have given themselves to wine in place of lust.
2.4: 2.4 That they love their husbands. Whom they naturally love with natural affection, let them love also with chaste love, namely that with modesty they render what is due to their husbands rather than demand it.
2.5: 2.5 That the word of God not be blasphemed. This can be referred to the old men and to all the above, as if he said: Exhort old men, and old women, and young women, to behave as I have said, which they ought to do so that the word of God not be blasphemed, etc.
2.7: 2.7 In all things, etc. For everyone who lives badly in the sight of those over whom he is set, as far as in him lies kills them; even if they live, they live by the mercy of God.
2.10: 2.10 That they adorn the doctrine of the Savior. This refers to all the above, namely to old men, and old women, and servants, as if he said: Exhort all the aforesaid to behave as prescribed, that they may so adorn in their acts the doctrine of the Savior, etc. Adorn. The adornment of the teacher is the honorable life of the disciple.
2.11: 2.11 For has appeared. As if he said: All must be admonished, because Christ was born for all, he excluded no one. Or, Grace, that is Christ, who is the grace of God. Or, the grace of God and Savior, etc., that is, our God and Savior, namely the Son of God, although invisible in the form of God, yet through grace appeared in the form of a servant.
2.13: 2.13 And the coming of the glory of the great God, etc. Who will come not in weakness as before, but in glory and power, to give rewards according to merits, he who in the first coming was so humble that he not only taught but even gave himself. A pursuer of good works, etc. Because for this Christ redeemed us, that pursuing a pure life and filled with good works, we may be able to be heirs of God.
2.15: 2.15 Reprove with all, etc. So that it not be received harshly, when it is known to be done for salvation.
3.1: 3.1 To every work, etc. As if he said: Admonish them to be slow to evil but ready for good, knowing that something must be rendered to each, because it is prepared for each.
3.3: 3.3 For we also were once. Even if some of us were philosophers, they still lacked true wisdom.
3.4: 3.4 The kindness, etc. By which he bestowed spiritual gifts on us abundantly.
3.10: 3.10 A heretical man. A heretic is one who attacks the law through the words of the law: for he builds up his own sense from the words of the law, so as to confirm the perversity of his mind by the authority of the law; such are to be avoided, because corrected too often they would be more practiced in evil.
3.11: 3.11 By his own judgment. He condemns himself who praises error and disparages the truth.
3.13: 3.13 Zenas the lawyer. He says this not because Apollos is more learned, but because he was of this profession in the Synagogue. Apollos. He was bishop of the Corinthians, who on account of a sedition stirred up against him by false apostles had departed with Zenas his companion to Titus the Cretan bishop. But the Corinthians now being calmed through Paul's letters, he commands Titus that before he comes to Nicopolis he send them on in the accustomed way, so that nothing be lacking to them for the journey. That nothing, etc. Therefore he commands that the necessary expenses be given them, because it was fitting that those who handed on spiritual things should not lack carnal things.
